## Introduction

Cutaneous beta- and gamma-HPVs act more like normal skin flora than disease-causing pathogens. They are acquired early in life, are ubiquitous in healthy adults, and persist as quiet, low-level infections [@antonsson2000; @doorbar2023]. At the DNA level, this viral reservoir is large and well-mapped. Shotgun metagenomics detected HPV in 61.3% of healthy skin samples [@ma2014], while skin swabs found beta-HPV in 92% of adults [@rollison2019sites]. This viral community is incredibly diverse, spanning 396 distinct types, 229 of which were previously unknown [@bzhalava2014]. However, these DNA figures alone cannot tell us whether any of this genetic material is actively transcribed.

This question matters because beta-HPV is a suspected cofactor in cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (cSCC), particularly in organ-transplant recipients [@howley2015; @rollison2019]. Three distinct, mutually compatible theories explain this role using the same data. Under the "hit-and-run" model, beta-HPV works with ultraviolet radiation, immunosuppression or chronic inflammation during early cancer development but becomes dispensable once the tumor forms [@viarisio2018; @dorfer2021]. Alternatively, the protective-immunity theory suggests T-cell immunity to regular papillomaviruses actively suppresses skin cancer, meaning viral loss reflects immune selection [@strickley2019; @lambert2021; @strickley2021]. This idea now includes evidence that viral colonization blocks mutant p53 clone expansion, with beta-HPV disappearing as those clones grow [@son2025]. A third theory requires neither premise, proposing that silence is simply the viral default because the beta-HPV genome uses E8\^E2 to repress its own expression, and cell transformation requires inactivating this repressor [@rehm2022]. Dispensability is a claim about requirement rather than persistence, so the decline follows from it only given a route to loss: ultraviolet-driven host mutations, for example in p53 or NOTCH, may make the viral oncogenes redundant, leaving the genome no longer selected for [@viarisio2018]. Ultimately, all three models predict declining viral activity from healthy skin to carcinoma, which is why measuring that decline more precisely cannot separate them.

Whether HPV is transcribed in cutaneous carcinoma has been studied directly, and the answers generally converge on "no." The original cSCC transcriptome study found no viral transcription [@arron2011]. This was mirrored in a study of 12 skin lesions at a median of 66 million reads [@hultin2019]. Similarly, a study of 345 post-transplant tumors at 35 million reads found transcription in only 15 cases [@arroyomuhr2021]. Another study of 23 risk-stratified biopsies showed zero viral expression, despite a 64% DNA positivity rate [@vandiver2021]. E6/E7 mRNA in situ hybridization supports these findings, showing expression in just 0.9% of 225 non-anogenital cutaneous SCCs [@fujimoto2019]. The literature is not entirely unanimous, however, as in situ hybridization previously demonstrated EV-HPV transcripts in 4 of 11 PCR-positive transplant cSCCs [@purdie2005]. Critically, what these existing studies lack is a proper denominator. Sample sizes remain small, ranging from only 11 to 345 specimens. Furthermore, four out of five studies looked exclusively at lesions without an unselected-skin comparator. The largest study was limited to formalin-fixed transplant material, and none scored productive replication.

Public archives can supply that missing denominator. Standard pipelines discard non-human reads, but these discarded sequences carry the viral signal [@edgar2022]. This approach has already been successfully applied to skin studies [@leiendecker2023; @bhargava2025]. However, the method is booby-trapped. HeLa-derived HPV18 contaminates archived data extensively [@cantalupo2015; @kazemian2015; @adey2013]. Additionally, sequencing depth and library chemistry both limit what any survey can reliably detect. Here, we re-mine public human RNA-seq data across the entire skin spectrum. We ask at what rate cutaneous HPV is transcribed, which specific types are present, and whether the infection is productive.
